title: The Elephant and the Rider: Why Good People Divide
book: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People are Divided by Politics and Religion
author: Jonathan Haidt
why: Haidt's first and most surprising claim is that our beliefs are driven primarily by intuition, with reason operating mostly to justify what we already feel.
text:
Haidt's first and most surprising claim is that our beliefs are driven primarily by intuition, with reason operating mostly to justify what we already feel. He calls this social intuitionism, and tells it with a memorable metaphor, the "Rider and the Elephant". The elephant is the vast, unconscious mind that in fact determines the direction, while the rider is the rational mind that thinks it is in charge and then works up explanations for decisions it never made. He is in good company: he points to David Hume and the biologist E. O. Wilson as thinkers who gave reason a "relatively low estimation", in contrast with Lawrence Kohlberg and his stages of moral reasoning, which put reason at the centre.

In the second part he lays out moral foundations theory: just as a tongue is organised to respond to different sorts of food, the human brain is organised to respond to several distinct kinds of moral violation. Haidt identifies six, the care or harm, the fairness or cheating, the loyalty or betrayal, the authority or subversion, the sanctity or degradation, and the liberty or oppression. In an interview he summed it up by saying morality "is at least six things, and probably a lot more than that". The practical upshot is a kind of compassion: because Republicans and Democrats tend to focus on different moral receptors, their views can look strange to one another, and Haidt says this leads to worse political tactics and worse decision making.

In the last part he introduces a hypothetical "hive switch", a capacity that turns a selfish human "chimp" into a "groupish" human "bee". Cultures and organisations, he notes, have techniques for making people identify with their groups, such as dancing, moving, and singing in unison. And there is a warmly personal note in the book: Haidt has been a liberal all his life, and working on these questions he has become more open to other points of view. Haidt is not alone in questioning the power of reason. Lee Harris, whom you have been reading, wrote The Suicide of Reason over the same suspicion, that civilisation runs on far more than logic. Where Harris keeps a wary eye on the ways group myth and ideology can turn against the civilisation that raised them, Haidt's aim is understanding and common ground. Both say something similar: if you want to know why people believe what they believe, you start with the feelings and the group, not with the arguments. Émile Durkheim, one of the founders of sociology, spent much of his career asking what creates the "we" in a society. He argued that it is shared rituals and collective experience that forge the solidarity which holds people together. Haidt's hive switch, with its dancing, moving, and singing in unison, is close to a modern restatement of Durkheim's insight that the group is born in the moments when people do something together. Where Harris keeps a wary eye on the power of the group, Durkheim and Haidt see the group as the soil in which community grows. Next time you feel very certain about something, notice whether it is your reasoning that speaks first, or your feelings. If your own moral foundations are doing some of the work, what might you be willing to ask of the people who feel just as strongly from a different place?

title: The Bonds That Hold Us: A Week in One Page
why: Monday opened with Lee Harris and his favourite trick: pressing something strange into a familiar shape.
text:
Monday opened with Lee Harris and his favourite trick: pressing something strange into a familiar shape. He begins with Montezuma, who had no category for the Spanish and so read them as the returning god Quetzalcoatl, a mismatch that proved fatal. Harris turns the same question on 9/11 and names what he calls a fantasy ideology: a belief that works like a stage, where the believer plays the hero of a cause he already accepts and treats everyone else as a prop. The example that stayed with me is Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, a war with no economic or strategic prize, demanded by the fantasy itself rather than serving any real end.

Tuesday met a very different voice in Carl Schmitt, the German legal theorist. His claim is blunt: the specifically political distinction is the one between friend and enemy. What keeps it alive is that the enemy is a role, not a name. Language, ethnicity, culture or religion turns political the moment a group uses it to define itself and becomes willing to defend that identity by force, and because each group decides for itself what counts as a threat, no outside judge can settle a truly political conflict.

Wednesday went back to the fourteenth century and a Tunisian scholar, Ibn Khaldun, who had already given social cohesion a name: asabiyyah, which his translator Franz Rosenthal rendered as "group feeling." It is the shared bond that lets a tribe defend itself and act as one. His bold claim is that this bond is cyclical: strongest at the birth of a civilisation, under the pressure of nomadic life, then thinning out as a dynasty grows settled and comfortable, and at last loosening into faction until a newer group with a fresher bond rises from the periphery.

Thursday brought in Karl Popper as a counterpoint. He names the story that historicists tell, that history obeys discoverable laws and so the future is already written, and traces it back to the doctrine of a chosen people, its two great modern faces being racialism and Marxism. His answer is the open society, a society whose first duty is the freedom of its citizens, where problems are fixed one by one in what he calls piecemeal social engineering, because if the future is genuinely open, the whole weight of responsibility falls back on us.

Friday closed the week back with Harris, in a short interview where he was careful with his word. He chose "civilisation" because it is value-free, describing a state of social organisation marked by tolerance, cooperation, a lessening reliance on violence, and above all stability. What struck me is that he calls it a transgenerational project, a trust that reaches across generations, and his clearest example is the Soviet Union, where when the state stopped being willing to apply terror, there was, in his words, "nothing there to hold them together." The week kept circling one question: what makes a group a group, and what keeps it together? Each thinker answered from a different end. Harris showed us the bonds that are staged rather than real, a fantasy that treats people as props. Schmitt gave us the raw minimum, a group defined by its willingness to fight alongside friends and against enemies. Ibn Khaldun named the bond itself, asabiyyah, and the quiet way that comfort wears it down. Popper warned against the story that pre-writes the future, because a society that believes its destiny is fixed quietly stops taking responsibility for the present. And Harris, in his closing interview, landed on the plainest version of all: civilisation as a transgenerational trust, the quiet glue of tolerance, cooperation and stability that you pass on.

What was most inspiring, honestly, was Ibn Khaldun. Fourteenth century, Tunisia, and he still saw that the very comfort a civilisation builds for itself is what slowly loosens the ties that hold it, and that the inheritance belongs to the people who still feel that bond most strongly. It is a sober and rather beautiful observation, and the one I kept returning to as I pulled the week together. Aristotle would have put the question differently, and it is a useful nudge. For him the real question was never just what holds the group together but what the group is for. In the Politics, the city is not merely a way of keeping people from perishing but a way of living well, and a life aimed only at survival is a diminished one. It sits comfortably alongside the week rather than against it: the bond matters, and it matters most when it is in the service of something worth living for. Here is the one question to take into the evening. Think of the group you most feel you belong to, the family, the team, the neighbourhood. What is the bond that actually holds it together, the shared history, the mutual trust, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it? If it were suddenly asked to hold a heavier weight than it was built for, what would you do to help it hold? There is no right answer. You only have to notice the bond, and decide what you would do to keep it strong.

title: What Holds a Society Together: Lee Harris in Ten Minutes
book: Our new epoch in history: 10 minutes with philosopher/political thinker/novelist Lee Harris
author: Bill Steigerwald (interviewing Lee Harris)
why: Harris starts by being careful with his word. He chose "civilization" because it is value-free, not a banner for us against them.
text:
Harris starts by being careful with his word. He chose "civilization" because it is value-free, not a banner for us against them. He defines it as a state of social organization marked by tolerance, by cooperation, by a lessening reliance on violence as a way of getting things done, and, most importantly, by stability. It is a picture of a society that has grown calmer rather than louder.

What strikes you is that he calls it a transgenerational project. A civilisation is not a snapshot; it is something you pass on. The values of your grandchildren should more or less reflect your own, and you hope they will not fall below the ethical baseline you set. There is real warmth in that: civilisation is trust that reaches across generations.

His best example comes from the collapse of the Soviet Union. The only reason to obey the orders there, he says, was fear of terror. When the state stopped being willing to apply terror, "there was nothing there to hold them together." The lesson he lands on is that a society has to have the ability to control its people in order to survive, and that the glue is far more fragile than most people assume. This is the quiet centre of Harris's whole project, the question of how a liberal society comes into existence and keeps existing. He gently pushes back on the assumption that when people get together, the first thing they do is construct a nice little society. That idea, civilisation as a deliberate and hard-won achievement that must be renewed by each generation, lands him in the company of the older thinkers who saw social order as something built rather than inherited. It is a sober and hopeful note for anyone who feels trust and shared institutions running thin: cohesion is a thing you make, not a thing you are born into. Ibn Khaldun saw something similar from the other end. The fourteenth-century historian wrote about asabiyyah, the social solidarity that binds a group together, and watched groups rise when that bond was strong and falter when it loosened. Both Harris and Ibn Khaldun are pointing at the same quiet fact: a society is only as durable as the bonds that hold it. Harris helps us see what a civilisation is; Ibn Khaldun helps us see how those bonds come and go. Look at the ties that hold your own community, workplace or circle of friends together. What shared habits, values or trusts make it more than a collection of strangers, and how do you notice when those bonds are quietly wearing thin?

title: The Future Is Not Written: Popper's Open Society
book: The Open Society and Its Enemies
author: Karl Popper
why: Today's reading is Karl Popper's defence of the open society, and it is a natural counterpoint to Lee Harris, because the two are working on the same ground: what happens when a people organise their lives around a story they believe is already written.
text:
Today's reading is Karl Popper's defence of the open society, and it is a natural counterpoint to Lee Harris, because the two are working on the same ground: what happens when a people organise their lives around a story they believe is already written. Popper gives that story a name and a method. He calls it historicism, 'the doctrine that history is controlled by specific historical or evolutionary laws whose discovery would enable us to prophesy the destiny of man.' The historicist believes the future has already been written, that if we can only read the laws of history we will know where everything is going. And that, Popper argues, is where the most dangerous ideologies come from: they promise a destination and then spend the present in the service of arriving there.

He traces the idea back to its oldest roots. In the first volume he argues that historicism grew 'out of the tribal form of social life', beginning with the doctrine of a chosen people whose destiny was fixed by God, and he finds its two great modern versions in racialism on the right and Marxism on the left. Both, he says, use the same method: an interpretation of history that claims to have found its law, and therefore to have a right to direct the present. That is a remarkable move, and worth sitting with. The promise of a guaranteed future is what makes these ideas so seductive, because it relieves us of a heavier burden: the open, unwritten, for all we know, possibility of what we might do next.

His answer is the one that gives the book its title. Popper calls it the open society: a society organised so that the protection of the citizens' freedom is the state's first duty, and where problems are fixed one by one rather than swept away in a single revolutionary act. He names this piecemeal social engineering, the practice of 'searching for, and fighting against, the greatest and most urgent evils of society, rather than searching for, and fighting for, its greatest ultimate good.' The quietly radical point is that the future is genuinely open. There is no law telling us what must happen. And if that is true, the whole weight of responsibility falls back on us, on the institutions we build and the arguments we are willing to test in public. Lee Harris spends his books naming the myths that organise our lives: the ideologies, the chosen narratives, the stories that make certain things unthinkable and certain acts inevitable. Popper, writing in the middle of a world war, identifies the same mechanism from the methodological side. For Harris the danger is that ideology turns people into characters in a fantasy. For Popper the danger is that historicism turns history into a prophecy. Both are myths, both mobilise, and both treat the present as a means to an imagined end. What each adds to the other is the answer. Harris helps us see the psychology and the culture; Popper helps us see the institutions. Between the two, we can tell where a myth is operating and how a free society might hold it at bay, by keeping the future open and by letting every argument be checked, criticised, and corrected before it is made law. It is worth knowing who Popper's first enemy is, because he places him in Athens rather than in a modern party. He reads Plato as the founder of the great historicist project. Confronted with the disorder of change, Plato's answer was to arrest it: to build a fixed state, run by philosopher kings, where the individual exists to serve the whole. Popper is generous where he can be. He praises Plato's analysis of social change even as he rejects his remedy, and he calls the generation of Athens before the Peloponnesian War the 'Great Generation', the moment critical discussion was invented and the open society first became possible. Plato and Popper, in other words, faced the same tremor in the ground: the fear that change leads to decay. Plato wanted to stop it. Popper wanted to build institutions that could keep going through it, one correction at a time. Read together, the two make the stakes clear. If the future really is not written by any law or destiny, what does that ask of the people and the problems in front of you this week? Which small thing, in your own corner, would you be willing to improve, without waiting for a grander plan?

title: The Glue That Holds Civilisation Together: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
author: Ibn Khaldun
why: Long before the phrase 'social cohesion' entered English political vocabulary, an Arab scholar in fourteenth century Tunisia had already given it a name.
text:
Long before the phrase 'social cohesion' entered English political vocabulary, an Arab scholar in fourteenth century Tunisia had already given it a name. Ibn Khaldun, writing his great work the Muqaddimah in 1377, called it asabiyyah, a word that in Arabic simply means 'group cohesiveness'. In the nomadic world he knew from experience, it was the bond that made a tribe able to defend itself, to share its burdens, and to act as one. When his translator Franz Rosenthal rendered the term into English, he chose the apt phrase 'group feeling', and it captures what Ibn Khaldun meant: that shared sense of belonging and purpose that makes people stick together not because they are forced to, but because they feel they belong to one another.

Ibn Khaldun made a bold claim that this bond is not static but cyclical. It is strongest at the very beginning of a civilisation, when a people is still shaped by the hard demands of nomadic life and the loyalty that comes with it. As a dynasty settles, becomes wealthy and comfortable, that group feeling slowly thins out. The rulers, far from the pressures that forged them, grow lax, their coordination weakens, and the shared bond 'dissolves into factionalism and individualism'. Eventually, says Ibn Khaldun, a new group with a fresher, stronger asabiyyah will rise from the periphery and take their place. He even offered a rough rule of thumb: no dynasty generally lasts more than three generations, roughly forty years each, because the bond that made it is not handed down intact.

What makes the idea memorable is its honesty. Ibn Khaldun was not writing a flattering account. He was saying that the very comfort a civilisation builds for itself is the thing that slowly loosens the social ties that held it together, and that the people who will inherit it will be the ones who still feel that bond most strongly. It is a sober and rather beautiful observation, and it has been read and argued over ever since. This connects to a question Lee Harris returned to again and again: what actually holds a society together, beyond law or economics or shared language? Tocqueville noticed a similar fragility in American society, and Durkheim gave the opposite condition, anomie, a name for the feeling of being untethered from the group. Ibn Khaldun's cycle, read generously, suggests that social cohesion is not a permanent feature of civilisation but something that must be renewed, generation by generation, or it quietly fades. Robert Putnam, writing in the 1990s, picked up the thread from a different end. His concept of social capital asked a more practical question: why do some communities trust each other and cooperate more easily than others? Where Ibn Khaldun described a natural cycle of rise and decay, Putnam was more interested in the institutions, habits and networks that can rebuild that trust within a society. The two perspectives complement each other: one describes the pattern, the other asks what can be done within it. Think about a group you belong to, a family, a community, a team, a generation of friends. What is the thing that actually binds it, the shared history, the mutual obligation, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it together? And what would happen if that bond were suddenly asked to hold a much heavier weight than it was built for?

title: Friend or Enemy: What Makes a People?
author: Carl Schmitt
why: Schmitt's central claim is memorable for its bluntness: "the specific political distinction … is that between friend and enemy." For him, the political is its own sphere, reducible to none of the others.
text:
Schmitt's central claim is memorable for its bluntness: "the specific political distinction … is that between friend and enemy." For him, the political is its own sphere, reducible to none of the others. Ethics sorts the good from the bad, the aesthetic the beautiful from the ugly, the economic the profitable from the unprofitable, but the political distinction belongs to none of these. Its measure is "the utmost degree of intensity … of an association or dissociation": on one side, the willingness to fight and die together with members of your own group; on the other, the willingness to kill simply because someone belongs to a hostile one.

What makes the idea durable is that the enemy is a role, not a name. The political is not tied to any particular marker. Language, ethnicity, culture, religion: any of them acquires political quality the moment a group uses it to define itself and becomes willing to defend that identity against others by force. If one distinction stops dividing people, another latches on and takes its place. And because each group decides for itself what counts as a threat to its way of life, a truly political conflict cannot be settled by an outside judge. It has to be lived through.

That last point carries the weight of his critique of liberalism. Schmitt thought the liberal hope, that all conflicts could be solved to everyone's advantage by civilisation, technology and amicable compromise, would leave life shallow and purposeless, and that a community no longer willing to draw a line between friends and enemies would wither in internal strife or be overwhelmed by one that still could. Schmitt drew on the line of thought running from Hobbes: a state is legitimate chiefly in so far as it can protect its members, and a state that can no longer name its enemies can no longer do that. Lee Harris made a cousin of the same move: his book Civilization and Its Enemies asks what happens when the ties that hold a civilisation together fray, and where its real enemies lie. Both thinkers are, in the end, diagnosticians. They want us to see that the groups we live in are real, that they have boundaries, and that the state of those boundaries decides more of our daily life than we like to admit. From the other end, the fourteenth-century Tunisian historian Ibn Khaldun saw the same dynamic. He argued that a group's social cohesion, the bond he called asabiyyah, is forged in opposition: communities rise when they are united against others, and decay when that bond relaxes. Where Schmitt was diagnosing how modern states think about themselves, Khaldun was describing how empires rise and fade over centuries. Read together, the two help us see that the enemy is not only a threat to a group, but part of what makes it. Think of a group you belong to, a neighbourhood, a workplace, a nation. Who or what do its members define themselves against? Does that answer feel natural, or a little unsettling?

title: A Stage, Not a Strategy: Harris on Fantasy Ideology
book: Al Qaeda's Fantasy Ideology: War without Clausewitz
author: Lee Harris
why: Harris opens with a story that belongs to no single nation or century. When the Spanish ships reached the coast of Mexico, Montezuma had no ready category for white men with steel and strange intentions.
text:
Harris opens with a story that belongs to no single nation or century. When the Spanish ships reached the coast of Mexico, Montezuma had no ready category for white men with steel and strange intentions. The only story his world offered was a myth, the return of the white god Quetzalcoatl, so that is what he expected, and the mismatch proved fatal. Harris's point is gentler than it first sounds: when an event is strange to us, we instinctively press it into our own familiar categories. The question he asks of the attacks of 9/11 is whether we were making exactly that mistake, reading a baffling act through the Clausewitzian idea that war is simply politics carried on by other means, a rational calculation with an end in view.

The essay's answer is a phrase of his own: a fantasy ideology. Harris first encounters it in a personal memory. In college in the late sixties, a friend planned to join a massively disruptive protest against the Vietnam War, and when Harris noted that it would likely backfire, the friend replied that it was, in his words, good for his soul. The demonstration was not about changing anyone's mind. It was a stage on which the protester played the hero of a cause he already believed in, and the commuters he lay down in front of existed only as props in the performance. Harris likens it to a game of Dungeons and Dragons played out in ideological symbols instead of medieval romances, and notes that the fantasist, in treating other people as props rather than as minds with wills of their own, is often surprisingly powerful.

The historical example that stays with you is the Italian conquest of Ethiopia. There was no economic or strategic gain to be had, and the diplomatic costs were severe. Ethiopia was a prop in the fantasy pageant of the new Italian Empire. The fantasy demanded that Italy conquer something, and the conquest was an end in itself rather than a means to one. Around it Harris gathers its siblings: the Jacobin dream of reviving the Roman Republic, Mussolini's Roman Empire, the antebellum South's sense of itself as the bearer of true civilisation, and, drawn from the French thinker Georges Sorel, the key insight Mussolini grasped. The Sorelian myth had to be presented as theater, with the audience's willing suspension of disbelief doing the work of persuasion. The essay stands quietly on a lineage worth knowing. William James asked what use a belief is when it cannot be scientifically demonstrated. The Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto extended that question to all the beliefs a society lives by. And the French thinker Georges Sorel, writing before the First World War, asked the further question of what happens when beliefs are deliberately manufactured, planted like seeds rather than catalogued like plants. Harris's contribution is to see ideology not as a description of the world but as a staging of it, and to notice that the make-believe can come to be an end in itself. The same essay defends an unfashionable word, the term evildoers, which he takes to strike exactly the right note. The lesson beneath it is the one worth carrying today: mistaking a symbolic drama for a rational strategy gets you all the wrong answers about what can be negotiated and what cannot. From a different quarter, Sigmund Freud looked at the same question from inside the group, asking what binds individuals to one another and to a leader. He found the answer in identification, a libidinal attachment he described as a kind of love. Harris shows the outside of the scene, the script and the props, while Freud shows the inside, the bond that keeps the audience in their seats. Together they suggest that a group's readiness to stop testing its story against reality has two faces, a play to perform and a tie to preserve. Is there a belief you hold, or a cause you once supported, that you would struggle to defend in a calm conversation? What do you think that belief was doing for you, describing the world, or staging it?
